1.name: Kamoni Williams
1.about: A towering generational interior presence with rare instincts, the freshman has already made Kamoni Williams look like a franchise-level anchor, using his 7’7” wingspan to hold opponents to 38% at the rim while flashing advanced passing feel for a big.

2.name: Miro Sanderson
2.about: Elite two-way indicators jump off the film, and few guards pressure the ball like Miro Sanderson, whose 37% shooting and transition vision make him the type of long, poised creator who would headline most draft classes.

3.name: Dubois Jackson
3.about: Controlling space comes naturally thanks to a 7’2” wingspan and strong timing, helping Dubois Jackson limit opponents to 41% at the rim. His athletic tools and rebounding activity highlight genuine two-way forward potential.

4.name: Dorian Payne
4.about: Floor spacing and interior toughness sit at the core of this stretch-four profile, where Dorian Payne blends 38% three-point shooting with disciplined rim defense, forming a modern matchup problem with real scheme versatility.

5.name: Jeremy Battle
5.about: Physical driving defines this backcourt prospect, with Jeremy Battle finishing 62% at the rim and thriving in isolation. His strength, footwork, and calm reads give him the foundation of a developing lead-guard creator.

6.name: Colby Lewis
6.about: Rim pressure comes easy for guards who absorb contact the way Colby Lewis does, leveraging a 6’8” wingspan to finish 63% at the rim while forcing fouls at a high rate for a young, physical scorer.

7.name: Brady Colby
7.about: Movement shooting stands out immediately for Brady Colby, whose 42% from deep and polished footwork give him clear spacing value. His instincts off the catch translate seamlessly into modern perimeter-heavy offensive systems.

8.name: Yameen Williams
8.about: Above-the-rim power defines this forward archetype, with Yameen Williams using a 7’3” wingspan to average strong block and putback numbers. His vertical finishing and defensive activity hint at impactful long-term upside.

9.name: Shamarion Jones
9.about: Defensive disruption drives this guard’s value, and Shamarion Jones uses a 7’0” wingspan to generate constant steals and deflections. His instincts give him a promising two-way profile as his offensive game continues developing.

10.name: Willie Broyles
10.about: Length-driven versatility anchors the projection of Willie Broyles, who produces deflections and contests at volume with a 7’0” wingspan. His rotational awareness pops on film, even as his offensive skill set remains a work in progress.

11.name: Matthew Jones
11.about: Physical perimeter pressure defines this guard, with Matthew Jones using a 6’8” wingspan to hound ballhandlers while knocking down threes as a rhythm shooter. His blend of defense and shot-hunting keeps him firmly in an intriguing two-way backcourt lane.

12.name: K.J. Franklin
12.about: Interior touch and strength highlight this young big, where K.J. Franklin leans on a 7’3” wingspan to convert 64% at the rim and rebound consistently. Mobility and rim protection remain swing skills for his long-term viability.

13.name: Tre Bluiett
13.about: Few freshmen apply downhill pressure like Tre Bluiett, whose explosive first step fuels a 69% rim-finishing mark. His transition impact is undeniable, though streaky shooting and raw playmaking keep him more projection than product.

14.name: Eusebiu Costache
14.about: European physicality shows up immediately in the slashing game of Eusebiu Costache, who finishes 61% inside the arc and defends multiple spots. Streaky shooting and inconsistent awareness remain areas needing refinement.

15.name: Haruto Takahashi
15.about: Shot-making polish stands out for Haruto Takahashi, drilling 40% from three with compact mechanics while handling connector duties. Limited length and strength cap his defensive ceiling, but his shooting gravity is immediately translatable.

16.name: Koen Phillips
16.about: Length and defensive pressure define this Australian wing prospect, where Koen Phillips uses a 6’11” wingspan to generate steals and bother creators. Shooting and half-court creation remain the developmental swing traits in his profile.

17.name: Omontae Miller
17.about: Rim protection and physicality anchor this freshman forward, as Omontae Miller blocks 2.3 shots per game and competes across frontcourt spots. His offensive game is raw outside finishing, leaving creation and shooting as long-term projects.

18.name: Aristotelis Margaritis
18.about: Modern 3-and-D traits headline Aristotelis Margaritis, who hits 36% from deep and guards the perimeter with functional strength. His limited creation and playmaking keep him firmly in a role-based wing projection.

19.name: Trezell Hamilton
19.about: Disruptive perimeter defense defines Trezell Hamilton, who posts strong steal rates while guarding top matchups. Limited three-point consistency and shaky creation keep him more of a defense-first wing.

20.name: Deyonze Burns
20.about: Two-way flashes highlight the profile of Deyonze Burns, who averages 1.8 blocks while handling the ball in space and scoring with touch inside. His jumper is early-stage, but his tools suggest long-term upside.

21.name: Quaylen Douglas
21.about: Mid-range control fuels this point guard’s identity, with Quaylen Douglas hitting 46% of his pull-ups and generating steals through active hands. His size limits some creation windows, but his craft offers real rotational potential.

22.name: Oskaras Vaškys
22.about: Craft and composure stand out in Oskaras Vaškys’ game, where he manipulates defenders with pacing and leverages a 2.4 assist-to-turnover ratio. Limited burst and inconsistent outside shooting temper his upside but fit a steady-playmaker archetype.

23.name: Rasheed Williams
23.about: Defensive versatility anchors Rasheed Williams’ value, using a 6’10” wingspan to take primary perimeter assignments while spacing the floor as a low-usage shooter. Limited creation keeps him firmly in a 3-and-D lane.

24.name: Aaron Marlow
24.about: Spot-up shooting and positional versatility define Aaron Marlow, whose 36% from deep pairs with reliable defensive effort across guard and wing matchups. Strength and off-the-dribble creation remain important developmental checkpoints.

25.name: Ja’Kaih Ellington
25.about: Interior disruption flashes early for Ja’Kaih Ellington, averaging 2.2 blocks while bringing power and vertical pop as a lob threat. His offensive skill set beyond finishing is raw, leaving shooting and post craft as long-term projects.

26.name: Yeray Cornejo
26.about: High-level vertical athleticism fuels Yeray Cornejo’s finishing, thriving on lobs, putbacks, and rim runs. His energy is undeniable, though defensive discipline and overall skill refinement remain necessary for pathway minutes.

27.name: Nidri Kinjambugi
27.about: Defensive chaos defines the forward profile of Nidri Kinjambugi, who jumps passing lanes and contests everything with a 7’0” wingspan. Limited shooting and creation leave him projected as a physical role-playing defender.

28.name: Colter Smith
28.about: Deep seals and soft touch drive Colter Smith’s interior offense, using his 7’6” wingspan to convert easy finishes around the rim. His mobility shortcomings and limited defensive range cap his ceiling significantly.

29.name: Anthony Motley
29.about: Stretch flashes from Anthony Motley come through in spot-up threes and vertical finishing at 7’0”, offering intriguing versatility. Strength, rebounding consistency, and defensive reads are still well behind his shooting development.

30.name: Matthew Drake
30.about: Floor-spacing reliability keeps Matthew Drake projecting cleanly, as the 6’8” forward hits catch-and-shoot threes and defends with toughness. Limited creation and average burst lower his ceiling but stabilize his role.

31.name: Jock Bellingham
31.about: Face-up scoring and connective passing drive Jock Bellingham’s value, using his 6’9” frame to operate from the mid-post while spacing the floor with soft touch. Defensive mobility concerns remain his biggest hurdle toward consistent rotation minutes.

32.name: Art Reynolds
32.about: Downhill craft fuels the offensive profile of Art Reynolds, who uses pace shifts and a strong frame to finish through contact. His jumper and playmaking remain inconsistent, keeping him projected as a secondary scoring option.

33.name: David Carter Jr.
33.about: Interior physicality defines David Carter Jr., who carves deep position and attacks the glass with force at 238 pounds. Limited vertical pop and shooting range contain his upside to a bully-ball, role-based interior scorer.

34.name: Tyler Bloxam
34.about: Rim protection and mobility highlight Tyler Bloxam’s defensive value, using a 7’3” wingspan to contest actions while covering ground well for his size. Limited strength, scoring touch, and shooting keep him primarily a defense-first depth big.

35.name: Carter Williams-Holliday
35.about: Energy and vertical pop help Carter Williams-Holliday compensate for his 6’7” height, finishing lobs and running the floor with nonstop activity. His limited shooting and raw defensive instincts restrict him to a play-finishing center projection.

36.name: Derrick Starks
36.about: Strong interior positioning and touch define Derrick Starks, who leans on a 254-pound frame to score efficiently around the basket. His limited mobility and defensive range keep him firmly in a ground-bound post scorer lane.

37.name: Treyvon Williams
37.about: Explosive straight-line drives and disruptive defense fuel Treyvon Williams’ projection, using a 6’9” wingspan to pressure ballhandlers and finish above the rim. Limited shooting and half-court creation place him squarely in an energy-wing role.

38.name: Ismael Lewis
38.about: Chaotic on-ball activity drives Ismael Lewis’ identity, thriving in transition and forcing turnovers with frenetic pressure. His shooting, decision-making, and control must improve to unlock his value as more than a change-of-pace guard.

39.name: Tyler Bridges
39.about: Vertical finishing and physical slashing highlight Tyler Bridges’ strengths, as he attacks gaps with force and elevates at the rim using a sturdy 218-pound frame. Limited shooting and passing awareness narrow him to a play-finishing forward role.

40.name: Jonah Williams
40.about: Steady game management defines Jonah Williams, who uses his length to defend guards and organize the offense with controlled passing. Scoring limitations and timid shooting cap his ceiling to a rotational facilitator archetype.

41.name: Tyler Gibbons
41.about: Interior disruption and vertical pop headline Tyler Gibbons’ impact, using a 7’0” wingspan and 225-pound frame to finish lobs and contest shots. Limited touch and raw footwork keep him a developmental play-finishing big.

42.name: Qua'sean Clark
42.about: Wing versatility shows up quickly with Qua’sean Clark, who spaces the floor as a confident catch-and-shoot option while using his 6’9” wingspan to defend multiple spots. Limited burst and on-ball creation keep him in a role-playing shooter mold.

43.name: Daouda Sylla
43.about: Straight-line explosiveness fuels Daouda Sylla’s slashing game, with his 6’11” wingspan helping him finish above defenders. His thin frame, streaky jumper, and limited playmaking leave him firmly in a developmental wing-guard trajectory.

44.name: Daniel Cleveland
44.about: Physical slashing and mid-range touch define Daniel Cleveland’s scoring approach, using his 208-pound frame to absorb contact while elevating cleanly into pull-ups. Limited playmaking and average shooting consistency keep him in a complementary scoring lane.

45.name: Jordan Morgan
45.about: Speed-driven offensive initiation anchors Jordan Morgan’s projection, as he pushes tempo, organizes actions, and plays with poise. His smaller frame, shaky rim finishing, and inconsistent jumper limit him to a depth point guard role.

46.name: Jaylen Blue
46.about: Pure downhill burst is the calling card for Jaylen Blue, who attacks the rim in transition and pressures defenses with pace. His lack of size, short wingspan, and streaky shooting keep him primarily a change-of-speed spark plug.

47.name: Trystan Marquez
47.about: Movement shooting and quick decision-making help Trystan Marquez thrive as a perimeter specialist, blending connective passing with spot-up accuracy. Limited athleticism and struggles finishing inside leave him projecting as a bench shooter and ball-mover.

48.name: Cristian Meléndez
48.about: Off-ball activity and defensive energy shape Cristian Meléndez’s profile, generating steals and contesting shots while hitting spot threes at a reliable clip. Limited creation and average burst keep him fitting cleanly as a 3-and-D rotation wing.

49.name: Trenton Washington
49.about: Strength-driven on-ball physicality highlights Trenton Washington, who bullies guards on drives and defends multiple positions with a sturdy frame. Limited burst and streaky shooting narrow his offensive ceiling, but his toughness defines his identity.

50.name: Brice Alvarez
50.about: Quick-twitch athleticism informs Brice Alvarez’s slashing and defensive disruption, using burst to pressure the rim and generate turnovers. His jumper and playmaking remain inconsistent, placing him squarely in a developmental energy-wing archetype.

51.name: Mehdi Marin
51.about: Spot-up shooting and connective passing fuel Mehdi Marin’s value, keeping the ball moving while punishing late rotations from deep. Limited burst, average length, and shaky rim finishing constrain him to a perimeter-oriented depth guard role.

52.name: Thomas Marchand
52.about: Length and mobility give Thomas Marchand defensive intrigue, using a 7’2” wingspan to block shots and finish lobs. His thin frame, limited strength, and raw offensive skill keep him firmly in long-term project territory.

53.name: Róger Meléndez
53.about: Explosive slashing defines Róger Meléndez’s approach, using a 6’9” wingspan to attack downhill and disrupt passing lanes. His thin frame, inconsistent jumper, and limited playmaking keep him a toolsy developmental wing-guard.

54.name: Shawn Hawk
54.about: Movement shooting is the foundation for Shawn Hawk’s projection, thriving off screens and spacing the floor reliably. His limited size, average athleticism, and difficulty finishing through contact cap him as a bench shooter.

55.name: Kristijan Šarić
55.about: Craft and pacing highlight Kristijan Šarić’s inside scoring and passing feel, navigating traffic with creativity. Limited burst, defensive concerns, and inconsistent perimeter shooting keep him projecting as a fringe rotation creator.

56.name: Drew Phillips
56.about: Poise and decision-making give Drew Phillips value as a steady offensive organizer, blending timing, passing, and spot-up shooting. His limited size, average athleticism, and shaky rim finishing restrict him to a depth-guard lane.

57.name: Miles Wright
57.about: Athletic bursts and defensive instincts help Miles Wright make energetic plays, blocking shots and attacking the rim with length. His jumper, decision-making, and consistency lag behind, placing him in a raw, toolsy developmental guard role.

58.name: Dion Marsh
58.about: Physical mid-post scoring defines Dion Marsh, who leans on his 249-pound frame to carve space and finish through contact. Limited burst, short wingspan, and below-the-rim athleticism restrict him defensively, leaving him a depth-big projection.

59.name: Imre Kovách
59.about: Efficient finishing and putback activity anchor Imre Kovách’s offensive value, using simple interior tools to convert around the rim. His limited mobility, narrow defensive range, and nonexistent shooting project him as an energy big.

60.name: Jonathan Baptiste
60.about: Mid-range touch and steady defensive versatility shape Jonathan Baptiste’s identity, creating clean pull-ups and guarding wings with a 6’9” frame. Limited burst, streaky three-point shooting, and modest playmaking keep him tracking as a rotation wing.
